name: Sicilian Defence
goal: As Black against 1.e4, you can play the Sicilian Defence: trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and fight back on the queenside.
intro: The Sicilian Defence, 1...c5, is the most popular answer to 1.e4. Black does not copy White in the centre. Instead the c-pawn fights for the d4 square, and when White opens the game with d4, Black trades that wing pawn for White's centre pawn. Black gets an extra centre pawn and an open road for the rooks on the c-file; White gets more space and quicker development. The games are sharp: White often plays in the centre or on the kingside, while Black fights back on the queenside.

parts.title: The Najdorf Variation
parts.keyIdea: Trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn, develop, castle, then use the c-file and queenside pawn moves to fight back.
parts.line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be2 e5 Nb3 Be7 O-O O-O

notes.text: 1...c5 controls d4 from the side instead of meeting e4 head on. If White plays d4, you can take with the c-pawn and swap a wing pawn for a centre pawn. 1...e5 is the other classical reply; 1...c5 leads to unbalanced positions where both sides have chances.
2...d6 opens a path for the c8-bishop and covers e5, so White cannot later chase a knight from f6 with e4-e5. 2...Nc6 and 2...e6 are the other main moves; all three get ready for White's d4.

White opens the centre with 3.d4. Take with 3...cxd4: this trade is the heart of the Sicilian. Your c-pawn is gone, but so is White's d-pawn, so you have two centre pawns (d6 and e7) against White's one (e4). The c-file is now half-open: none of your pawns stands on it, so your rooks can use it.
4...Nf6 develops with a threat: the knight attacks the e4 pawn, so White has to spend a move defending it. 5.Nc3 is the usual answer.

5...a6 is the Najdorf Variation. It looks slow, but it takes the b5 square away from White's knights and bishop (a knight on b5 would hit d6), and it prepares ...b5 to gain space on the queenside, where your c-file already points.

6...e5 pushes White's knight out of the centre and gives you a share of d4 and f4. The price is a hole on d5 and a pawn on d6 that no other pawn can protect. Black's answer is to keep d5 under control with pieces, such as the f6 knight and later a bishop on e6.
The knight has gone back to b3. 7...Be7 develops the bishop, protects the d6 pawn and clears the way for castling. 7...Be6 first, aiming at d5 at once, is also played.

8...O-O puts your king safe before the fight starts. The usual plan from here is ...Be6 to watch d5, a knight to d7 or c6, a rook to c8 on the half-open c-file, and ...b5 or ...a5 to push on the queenside, while White tries to use the d5 square.
